alt: A contract is discharged when the parties’ obligations end, by performance, agreement, breach or frustration. Performance and agreement are the normal, peaceful endings; breach and frustration are where disputes arise and where Paper 2 questions concentrate.
caption: Performance and agreement end a contract peacefully; breach and frustration produce the disputes.

alt: The strict rule from Cutter v Powell (1795) requires complete and exact performance. Exceptions: substantial performance (Hoenig v Isaacs) but not where defects are serious (Bolton v Mahadeva); divisible contracts; freely accepted part performance (contrast Sumpter v Hedges); prevention (Planché v Colburn); and refused tender of performance (Startup v Macdonald).
caption: Exact performance is the rule; five exceptions soften it.

alt: An agreement to end a contract needs consideration. In bilateral discharge both parties still have obligations, so mutual release is consideration on both sides. In unilateral discharge one party has already performed, so the other must give something new or use a deed: accord and satisfaction. Contracts can also end under their own terms or by novation.
caption: Ending a contract by agreement still needs consideration, unless a deed is used.

alt: Every breach gives a right to damages, for example breach of a warranty (Bettini v Gye). Only a repudiatory breach gives the innocent party the option to treat the contract as ended: breach of a condition (Poussard v Spiers), a breach of an innominate term that deprives them of substantially the whole benefit, or renunciation. In Hong Kong Fir a ship unseaworthy for some weeks of a two-year charter was not serious enough.
caption: Every breach gives damages; only a repudiatory breach gives the option to end the contract.

alt: When a party announces before performance that they will not perform, the innocent party may sue immediately (Hochster v De La Tour) or wait for the date of performance. Waiting carries risk: in Avery v Bowden war frustrated the contract and the right to sue was lost. In White and Carter v McGregor the innocent party performed and claimed the price, given a legitimate interest.
caption: The innocent party chooses: sue at once, or keep the contract alive and bear the risk.

alt: A contract is frustrated by an event after formation, no one’s fault, that makes performance impossible, illegal or radically different (Davis Contractors). Frustrating events: destruction (Taylor v Caldwell), death or incapacity (Robinson v Davison; Condor v Baron Knights), supervening illegality (Fibrosa), government intervention (Metropolitan Water Board v Dick Kerr) and purpose defeated (Krell v Henry). Not frustrated: purpose only partly defeated (Herne Bay), more difficult or expensive (Davis; Tsakiroglou), self-induced (Maritime National Fish; The Super Servant Two), or foreseen or covered by a term.
caption: Frustration is narrow: a harder, dearer or self-induced problem does not end the contract.

alt: At common law loss lay where it fell, and Fibrosa allowed recovery only on a total failure of consideration. Under the 1943 Act, s 1(2) makes money paid before the event recoverable and money payable cease to be payable, with a discretion to allow expenses up to that amount (none were allowed in Gamerco). Under s 1(3) a party who obtained a valuable non-money benefit may have to pay a just sum (BP v Hunt).
caption: The Act unpicks payments fairly; any allowance for expenses is the court’s choice.

alt: Kemi paid a £1,000 deposit with £2,000 due on the night; the lead singer is injured. The contract is probably frustrated because incapacity of the key performer makes performance radically different (Robinson v Davison; Condor v Baron Knights). Under s 1(2) the £1,000 is recoverable and the £2,000 ceases to be payable; the court may let the band keep up to £300 for expenses if just.
caption: Frustrated, then s 1(2): deposit back, balance cancelled, expenses at the court’s discretion.
